this work, that the whole operation of its art is sufficiently contained in general chapters, in universal discourse, without any diminution. By God, he who has worked according to this book will rejoice to have found for himself the true end of this art. But know, dearest, that he who has ignored the natural principles in himself, this man is already very far removed from our art, since he does not have a true root upon which he might found his intention. And he who has known his principles of nature, and all the causes of minerals, has not yet attained the true end and profit of this most occult art, although he has an easier access to the principles of this art than he to whom ignorance falls upon his intention regarding the mode of this our work, and he is little removed from the entry of the art. But he who has known the principles of all things, and the causes of minerals, and the mode of generation, which consists of the intention of nature, is indeed little removed from the completion of the work, without which, however, our science cannot be perfected, since art cannot imitate nature in all works, but imitates it as it rightfully can. Dearest son, therefore, we disclose a secret to you, that in this the artists err, that they desire to imitate nature in all the differences of the properties of action. Labor therefore to study in our volumes, and strive to revolve them most often in your mind, so that you may acquire the true intention from the mode of our speech, because in them you will find that upon which you ought to found your mind, and you will know from them how to repel errors from yourself, and in what you may be able to imitate nature in the artifice of your work.

->Division of this first book into four parts. Chapter II.<-

We shall therefore briefly place before you first all the impediments, by which the artist is hindered in the work, lest he attain the true end, and we shall also speak of the conditions of the artist of this art. Secondly, we shall dispute against the ignorant and the sophists, who, because of their ignorance and lack of skill, while inquiring into the magistery and profit of this art, kill the art and contend that it is nothing. We shall place all their arguments, and afterwards we shall destroy them most evidently: so that it may be openly clear to the prudent that their sophisms contain no truth. Thirdly, we shall dispute over the natural principles, which are of the intention of nature: and therein over the mode of their generation and commixture with one another by the work of nature, and over their effect, according to the opinion of the ancient Philosophers. Fourthly, we shall show the principles which are to the intention of this our work, in which we can imitate nature, and the mode of mixing, and altering, namely of the appropriate nature with its causes, to be reduced to the intent of our work.

->FIRST PART OF THIS FIRST BOOK ON THE IMPEDIMENTS,<-
->by which artists are hindered, so that they might not attain the true end of this art.<-
->Division of the impediments. Chapter III.<-

THERE are therefore, generally, two impediments supervening to this work: namely, natural impotence, and the lack of necessary expenses, or occupations and labors. However, we say that natural impotence is manifold. Namely, on the part of the artist's organ, and on the part of the soul. Also manifold on the part of the artist's organ. Either because the organ becomes weak, or is wholly corrupt. Finally, from the impotencies of the soul, in many ways, either because the soul becomes perverse in the organs, because the organs have no rectitude or reason in themselves, like the soul of a madman, or a fool. Or because it becomes fantastic, easily susceptible to contrary forms unduly, and extensible from one knowable thing to its opposite suddenly, and from one similarly to its opposite.

Per Deum, qui secundum hunc librum operatus fuerit, verum finem huius artis se adinuenisse lætabitur. Sed scias carissime, quòd qui principia naturalia in seipso ignorauerit, hic iam multum remotus est ab arte nostra, quoniam nō habet radicem veram, supra quam intentionem suam fundet. Et qui principia sua sciuerit naturæ, & causas mineralium omnes, nondum tamen adeptus est verum finem & proficuum huius artis occultissimæ, habet verò faciliorem aditum ad artis huius principia, quàm cui ignorantia cadit super intentionem eius de modo huius nostri operis, & hic parum remotus est ab artis introitu. Qui verò sciuerit omnium principia, & causas mineralium, & generationis modum, qui ex intentione naturæ consistit, parum quidem aufertur ab eo de operis complemento, sine quo tamen non potest scientia nostra perfici, quoniam ars imitari non potest naturam in omnibus operibus, sed imitatur eam sicut rite potest. Carissime igitur fili, secretum tibi pandimus, quòd in hoc artifices errāt, quòd natura in omnibus differentiis proprietatum actionis imitari desiderant. Labora itaque studere in nostris voluminibus, & ea sæpissime in mente tua reuoluere nitaris, vt intentionem ex nostræ loquelæ modo veram acquiras, quía in eis inuenies, super quæ mentem tuam fundare debeas, & scies ex eis errores à te repellere, & in quibus imitari naturam possis in tui operis artificio.

Ponemus igitur tibi breuiter primò impedimenta omnia, quibus in opere impeditur artifex, ne verum finem adipiscatur, dicemus etiam conditiones artificis huius artis. Secundò verò disputabimus contrà ignorantes & sophistas, quòd propter suam ignorantiam & imperitiam, huius artis magisterium & proficuum inquirendo, artem interimunt, & eam nullam esse contendunt. Ponemus autem omnes rationes illorum, & postea ipsas destruemus euidentissime: ita vt prudentibus fatis apertè pateat, nullam illorū sophismata veritatem continere. Tertiò disputabimus super principijs naturalibus, quæ sunt de intentione naturæ: & ibidem super modo generationis & mistionis eorum adinuicem ab opere naturæ, & super eorum effectu, secundum antiquorum Philosophorum sententiam. Quartò verò monstrabimus principia, quæ sunt ad intentionem huius nostri operis, in quibus imitari naturam possumus, & modum miscendi, & alterādi, scilicet congruum naturæ cum causis suis, ad intentum nostri operis reducendis.

SVNT ergo impedimenta huic operi superuenientia, duo generaliter: Naturalis scilicet impotentia, & necessariæ impensæ defectus, vel occupationes & labores. Naturalem tamen impotentiam multiplicem esse dicimus. Ex parte scilicet organi artificis, & ex parte animæ. Ex parte etiam organi artificis multipliciter. Vel quia organum fit debile, vel ex toto corruptū. Ex animæ denique impotentijs multipliciter, vel quia fit anima peruersa in organis, propter organa nihil rectitudinis, vel rationis in se habens, sicut anima insani, vel fatui. Vel quia fit fantastica, contrariarū facile formarum susceptiua indebite, & de vno scibili ad eius oppositum extensiua subito, & de vno vel ad eius oppositum similiter.

From three great circles of the sphere inscribed in such a way that each is cut into four equal parts, and into the ends of these the poles of the circles fall—having been assumed three times—presupposing that both the circles and any given points on them have all their force and essence from the poles, and gathering from these: if the triple force of the poles be conceived as poured out from the ends of the four parts into the circle, there arise in that same circle four times three virtues of the same nature. A sufficiently obscure emptiness! Let it suffice to have noted the falsity of the hypothesis. The circumference, which Morinus, along with the common crowd of Astrologers, calls a circle, contrary to *Euclid’s Elements*, Book 1, definition 15, and *Theodosius’s Spherics*, Book 1, definition 5, is the limit of a circle, which is generated from the motion of a straight line, of which one end remains at rest at a given point, while the other is moved around until the beginning of the motion returns. He asked the two bailiffs to let him go, but they refused, acting with great arrogance. Wang was angry and wanted to argue with them, but his brother stopped him, saying, "This is an official order; we should follow the law. Wang grabbed his brother's arm and cried out, losing his voice. The bailiff became enraged and violently pulled the rope around his brother's neck. The brother fell, and seeing this, Wang was filled with a burning anger he could not contain. He drew his ceremonial sword and immediately severed the head of the bailiff. Another bailiff shouted, and Wang severed his too. The woman was greatly shocked and said, "Killing a government officer is an unpardonable crime. If you delay, the disaster will reach you. Please find a boat immediately and head north to return home. Do not go out or mention this; keep the door shut for seven days, and I guarantee there will be no trouble." Wang then pulled his brother away, bought a small boat at night, and crossed the river north in a hurry. When he returned, he saw mourners at his door and realized his brother had indeed died. He locked the door and went in to see, but his brother had already passed away. He entered the room, and the deceased had already been revived.

### XXXI.

*Ex pituita originem traxisse, constat ex natura pituitosa, colore articuli albicante, dolore obtuso perseverante cum tumore œdematoso, ex esca antea ingesta, ultimò ex paroxysmo <sup>a</sup> singulis diebus redeunte.*
*a Pered. in Paschal. l. 1. c. 61.*

### XXXII.

*A melancholia rarò fit podagra; si tamen originem trahat ab humore atro, mala est, tùm quia multò magis turbat quàm aliæ; tùm quia diutiùs durat, nec ita medicamentis cedit. Notæ, quibus proditur sunt dolor profundus cum gravitate, color nigricans, temperies frigida & sicca, ætas ad senectam vergens, circuitus acerbationum quarto die redeunt: urinæ utplurimùm tenues & aquosæ in principio, postea atræ & modicè crassæ, & quod subsidet in eis, aliquando fuscum est, aliquando verò mixtum, teste Paul. l. 3. c. 78.*

### XXXIII.

*Ex varia denique permixtione humorum, si podagra prodeat, vario modo signa permixta exurgent.*

### XXXIV.

*Quod ad prognosin attinet, ex prædictorum natura atque conditione innotescit. Generatim tamen affirmandum, omnem podagram esse difficilem curatu.*

### XXXV.

*Curari tamen possunt juvenes, <sup>a</sup> quanquam hereditario jure illam habuerint, & illi, <sup>b</sup> in quibus circa articulos calli tophacei concreti nondum comparent, qui laborem amant, & alvum obedientem habent, hi sanè Medicum prudentem nacti, salvi fieri poterunt.*
*a Felix Plater, in observ. l. 2. p. 473. b Hipp. 6. aph. 49. & 55.*

### XXXVII.

Dolores podagrici utplurimùm Vere et Autumno moventur, ut docet Hippocrates 6. aphorismo 55. Quibuscunque verò morbi podagrici fiunt, ii sedatâ spacio 40. dierum inflammatione finiunt, modò (ut ait Galenus in commentariis) Medicus in suo opere non aberraverit, et æger illi in omnibus obedierit.

### XXXIIX.

Aliàs ratione viæ et exitus ipsius, malum hoc quatuor modis utplurimùm terminatur: aut enim resolvitur, et hoc sæpiùs; aut maturatur, sed rarò; aut induratur aliquando; aut transfertur ad membra nobilia, unde multis in hydropicum morbum, quibusdan in asthma, ut testatur Aëtius, desiit.

### XXXIX.

Ex his jam dictis apparet, diversis à causis podagram originem trahere, diversimodè etiam finiri: Ratione originis, aliam esse calidam, ut quæ à sanguine et bile; aliam frigidam, ut quæ à pituitâ et atra bile oritur; aliam mixtam naturam obtinere, pro ratione materiæ causantis; aliam curabilem existere, aliam verò nullo modo.

### XL.

Quæ autem curabilis est, et medicinam admittit, secundùm methodicam curandi rationem, quæ indicationibus

### XXVI.

With the sources of the causes set forth, two differences emerge, derived from the variety of the transmitting parts and of the troublesome matter. Since these are manifest from the aforesaid, I shall proceed to the signs.

### XXVII.

In general, this affection is easily recognized, inasmuch as the patient himself perceives an expansive pain around the joints of the feet; then there is present a tumor, inability to walk, and restlessness around the feet, so that he finds no place where he may peacefully rest his feet.

### XXIIX.

You will know the humor causing the gout from many things: from the <sup>a</sup> nature of the patient, from the color of the joint, the sensation of pain, and what helps and what harms.

<sup>a</sup> Pered. in schol. Paschal. l. 1. c. 61. Mercurial. l. 4. c. 3.

### XXIX.

We shall know that gout is made from blood by the nature of the patient, if they are of a sanguine temperament; by the redness of the joint together with severe pain; by past life; by the unnatural detention of blood in the womb, or hemorrhoids; by plethora; by flourishing age; by the spring season; and by what helps and what harms.

### XXX.

A bilious gout is shown by <sup>a</sup> sharper pain, yellow and bilious urine, <sup>b</sup> the color of the joint inclining toward lemon-yellow, <sup>c</sup> acute pain similar to a stinging object, a bitter taste in the mouth, a less evident tumor, youthful age, and a hot and dry temperament; the regimen of diet generating bile has preceded; <sup>d</sup> exacerbations of the pain occur every third day.

<sup>a</sup> Paschal. l. 1. cap. 61. <sup>b</sup> Paul. Aeginet. l. 3. c. 78. <sup>c</sup> Mercurial. l. 4. c. 3. <sup>d</sup> Pered. in schol. Paschal. l. 1. c. 61.

### XXVII.

In genere facilè cognoscitur hic affectus, quandoquidem æger ipse dolorem extensivum circa articulos pedum percipit, deinde adest tumor, ambulandi impotentia, inquietudo circa pedes, ita ut nullum locum inveniat, ubi pacatè pedes deponat.

### XXIIX.

Humorem facientem podagram ex multis cognosces, ex <sup>a</sup> natura ægri, ex colore articuli, doloris sensu, juvantibus & nocentibus.

<sup>a</sup> Pered. in schol. Paschal. l. 1. c. 61. Mercurial. l. 4. c. 3.

### XXIX.

Cognoscemus podagram fieri à sanguine, ex natura ægri, si sanguinea sit, ex rubore articuli simul cum gravi dolore, ex anteacta vita, detentione sanguinis præter naturam in utero, vel hæmorrhoidibus, plethorâ, ætate floridâ, tempore verno, juvantibus & nocentibus.

### XXX.

Biliosam ostendunt, <sup>a</sup> dolor acutior, urina flava & biliosa, <sup>b</sup> color articuli ad citrinum vergens, <sup>c</sup> dolor acutus rei pungenti similis, sapor in ore amarus, tumor minùs evidens, ætas juvenilis, temperamentum calidum & siccum; præcessit ratio victus bilem generans, <sup>d</sup> doloris exacerbationes fiunt de tertio in tertium diem.

Tumor itaque cùm ex fientium morborum sit numero, atque

### X L I I.

Inter antecedéntes causas humor in toto corpore vel parte
mandante redundans, vacuans auxilium postulat. Idem

### XIX.

When an heir lends money bequeathed to another, he seems to give it tacitly under this condition, if the legatee abstains from the legacy, which condition if it comes to pass, the loan will be confirmed retroactively from the day the inheritance was entered.

<margin>
Law 8, at the verse "item si" <gloss>likewise if</gloss>. Although otherwise an obligation is not usually born except from the time of the existing condition, here it is otherwise, because a legacy is always understood to have been acquired from the day the inheritance is entered, either by the legatee or by the heir.
</margin>

### XX.

A condition defers the obligation of a loan, which is a true condition and contains an uncertain outcome, not one which is referred to the present or past time. For the truth of the thing and of nature is regarded, not our ignorance.

<margin>
a Law 39, paragraph "Sub conditione" <gloss>Under a condition</gloss>, on verbal obligations.
b Law 37.
c Law 38, Law 30, paragraph "suum" <gloss>its own</gloss>, on acquiring an inheritance. It does not hinder Law 28, paragraph "si" <gloss>if</gloss>, on judgment. For our knowledge or lack thereof is looked at when the matter is brought into judgment and must be proved to the judge.
d Law 28, it is otherwise when only the competent right is questioned.
</margin>

### XXI.

Beyond the condition, pledges and other obligations also not rarely accompany a loan.

### XXII.

If the creditor is not sufficiently secured by a pledge, he does not lose the quantity of that debt for which the pledge does not suffice.

<margin>
Law 28, Law 8, Code "if a certain thing is sought." It is otherwise, however, when one is sent by the praetor into possession of the debtor's goods, or when pledges are taken by judgment to settle a debt. For in this case, he who seeks the pledge to be adjudged to him is seen to settle the debt as if by pact, Law 15, paragraph "si pignora" <gloss>if pledges</gloss>, on the thing judged.
</margin>

De quo Justinus liber 8. capite 1 Haut levius periculum timendum ex illa Avaritia rebus quæ cernitur in privatis, cum scilicet vel singuli ex Magistratibus, vel totus ordo; Magistratuum privatorum bona ad se vi, dolo, & sub prætextu quodam trahunt.

## XIII. 
Hæc verò **Avaritia** cum præ reliquis frequens existat causa ruinæ, tutissime Rex faciet, si parva tributa per partes, consentientibus statibus, demonstrata rei nummariæ necessitate exigat, ordinaria conservet, nova haud facile imperet. Adamus Conzenius liber 9. Politicorum capite 8. §. 4. Præsertim cum in Principibus & Rempublicam gubernantibus nullum tetrius reperiatur vitium **Avaritiâ**. *Habere enim quæstui Rempublicam, non modò turpe est, sed sceleratum etiam atque nefarium*, inquit Cicero. Imo ipsi etiam repugnat naturæ; hinc idem 

> detrahere aliquid alteri, inquit, & hominis incommodo suum augere commodum, magis est contra naturam quàm mors, quàm paupertas, quàm dolor, quàm cætera quæ possunt aut corpori accidere aut rebus externis. Nam tollit convictum hominum & societatem: Si enim sic erimus affecti, ut propter suum quisque emolumentum spoliet aut violet alterum disrumpi necesse est eam, quæ maxime est secundum naturam, humani generis societatem.

XI. And no less effective and much more frequent is the cause of changes in Commonwealths: the Avarice of those who rule. Aristotle noted this in *Book 5 of his Politics, chapter 3: Pride, he says, and Avarice of those who govern men provoke them against themselves and against the state of that Commonwealth which allows these things to occur.* And Adam Conzen says in *Book 7 of his Politics, chapter 22, §. 18: It is also a marvelous and true saying of sacred oracles that Avarice is the mother and root of all evils in Commonwealths, especially when it inheres in the souls not of private individuals, but of judges.* For where Avarice reigns, there good laws are oppressed: For *according to Tacitus, their help is invalid where they are disturbed by force, bribery, and finally money:* But where good laws are exiled, there everything rushes toward the worse. For just as our bodies without the mind, so a city without law cannot use its parts as nerves, blood, and limbs. Plautus confirms this in his *Trinummus*, when he says: *It is all over with that State in which morals have brought the laws under their own power, and have miserably fixed them to the wall with iron nails.*

XII. Moreover, this Avarice is accustomed to be exercised both in public and in private matters. To this pertain the iniquitous exactions of taxes, which rarely enrich Princes, often are their destruction, and are profitable only to the officials. The example of Achaeus, King of the Lydians, teaches this; the Lydians hung him by his feet for being too greedy in demanding taxes, so that his head was immersed in the Pactolus, that he might thus satisfy his thirst with gold-bearing water. That matter concerning Johanna VIII, the Papess, whom they say feigned her sex to obtain the Pontificate, seems a fiction to many. They err vehemently who say that Wittikind was King of the Saxons, since he was only a Duke of war. Nor does the testimony of Dithmar, who is to be interpreted through Wittekind, stand in our way here. Johannes *Garzias of Bologna* is a recent writer who calls him King, according to *Goldastus*. Nor is *Sagittarius* consistent with himself in this argument, nor, before him, that otherwise very learned man *Reineccius*, and most recently Johannes *Ludwig Schönleben* in a polemical dissertation on the first origin of the Habsburg-Austrian house, published at Ljubljana in the year 1680, in which, having followed the common herd of historians, he also calls Wittekind the Great King of the Saxons.

### IX.

No Roman Emperor wrote himself as Saxon, nor did Justinian himself, although he wrote himself Frankish, Alemannic, and Germanic. For that no one wrote himself Saxon, all the coins, inscriptions, and Roman histories, devoid of such a title, show. For the first, Charlemagne calls himself *dominator* <gloss>ruler/lord</gloss> of the *Saxons*, using *dominator* in the sense of that age, for a supreme Prince.

### §. 17.

Finally, I will not say that all doctors refer to this, which is contained in Genesis 49. Where Jacob, being about to die, predicted what would happen to his sons after much time; and when he had come to Dan, he says:

> *Dan shall judge his people; he shall be a serpent in the way, and an adder in the path, biting the heels of the horse, so that his rider falls backward.*

This they interpret concerning Samson, for he bit, as it were, the foot of the horse when he overturned the column, that is, the foot of the upper room, and struck down the rider, that is, the assembly of the Philistines, with the ruin of the roof. However, no judge from the tribe of Dan had appeared before Samson, as we have already noted above, and no one from all the judges was previously designated and as it were publicized by GOD before he was born, except for Samson alone. From the things already alleged, it can be most clearly evident that the object of Samson's act is devoid of all malice, and it is not <term>autocheiria</term> <gloss>self-killing/suicide</gloss>, nor did it happen by chance, but was a work of the greatest moment, which had already been predicted so many centuries before by the most holy Patriarch Jacob. To say nothing further of the fact that, according to the theologians, he was a type of Christ in this, who laid down his life for his sheep; not to mention the things brought forward in the sacred history itself regarding the praise of this act, where it is not so much blamed as praised, when it is said with a certain admiration that he killed more in dying than he had killed alive before; as can be seen in Judges 16, verse 30. Finally, it completes both sides of the matter that in Hebrews 11, Samson is read to be included in the catalog of the Saints who by faith conquered kingdoms and worked righteousness. In faith, however, as is known, the end, not the battle, crowns.

Ex quibus jam allegatis luculentissimè patescere potest, objectum facti Simsonis omnis malitiæ esse expers, nec esse αὐτοχειρίαν, nec accidisse fortè fortunâ, sed opus maximi momenti, quod ante tot secula jam erat prædictum à sanctissimo Patriarchâ Jacobô. seed: There are large-scaled fish that can swallow a boat. At that time, everyone departed and took off, not knowing that the large fish had already swallowed the boat and it had sunk. Therefore, the wise do not covet that flavor, so that they may remain secure. Good man, the <term>Zhenren</term> <gloss>Perfected Person</gloss> and the youth do not wish to covet the flavor of the defilements, and it is also like this. Good man, when the <term>Zhenren</term> and the youth dwell in the Haikong <gloss>Ocean-Emptiness</gloss> Treasury and contemplate the suffering of the defilements, it is also like a wise man observing the fish and the boat, not giving rise to joy. Good man, a person’s life, aging, and decline are constant and eternal; there is no happiness. Coveting love and desire is like water in a pond where a lotus grows; it opens and flourishes, very lovely and enjoyable, but when it encounters the frost and electricity of heaven, it is all destroyed. Good man, a person’s life and happiness, loving color and desire, and the body falling into the suffering of the three paths <note>referring to the three lower realms: hell, hungry ghosts, and animals</note>, it is also like this. It is like a broken axle that is no longer of any use; aging is also like this, one cannot return to being young. It is like someone on land whose heart constantly misses the water; a good man is also like this, although he has an aged countenance, he constantly remembers his youth. It is like the lotus in the pond under the autumn moon that everyone loves to see, but suddenly it withers and turns yellow, and people abandon and despise it. Good man, the strength of youth and the color of one’s prime are also like this; they are all loved and enjoyed by everyone, but suddenly one becomes an old guest, and what people despise is also like this. Good man, it is like sugarcane, once it has been pressed, there is no more flavor. Good man, the flourishing of youth is also like this; once one is covered by an aged countenance, there is no passion. Good man, it is like a polished mirror, day by day it must be held and not separated from the heart and wisdom. Good man, a person is also like this; youth is flowery and orderly, old age is declining and weak, the form and spirit are withered and wretched, constantly thinking of the time of youth and not separating from heart and wisdom. Good man, the <term>Zhenren</term> and the youth secretly practice the One-Vehicle Ocean-Emptiness Precious Treasury, observing the suffering of sickness, constantly having fear and terror, and thoughts of being insecure. Good man, it is like an enemy, one constantly has worry and sorrow. Good man, it is also like this, observing the defilements, one constantly has worry and sorrow. It is like rice stalks being infested with insects and then dying; a good man is also like this; when a person has an epidemic sickness, it is difficult to cure, and in an instant, they die. It is like the King's carriage with the high minister walking in front and the King dwelling behind; when they reach the enemy in battle, the King and minister pursue and cannot be separated. ### XIX.

In what way we now also use the word "Disparatum," to denote, first, that which agrees with another or others in a proximate Genus. This is: 1. A Species different from another or others by opposite differences of a divided Genus. For example, man in relation to a beast or brute, etc. 2. An individual in respect to another or several individuals of the same or different species, yet of the same Genus. Consider Pythagoras in relation to Socrates, Bucephalus, this dog, etc. Secondly, that which differs from another or others in a proximate Genus. That is: 1. A Species different from another of a different Genus, or from species of different Genera. Such as man compared to a tree, magnitude, science, similarity, etc. 2. An individual compared with another or several individuals of different species of different Genera, for example, Aristotle with the multitude of his books, with his Physics, with his equality to Plato, etc. Thirdly, that which agrees with another or others, not indeed in any Genus, but nevertheless in a most universal concept. <margin>al-Shalubini said: The correct view is that this is permissible, and it is the well-known and supported position. I say: He has already indicated this in the poem.</margin>

<margin>Used in its entirety, it is omitted, as in his saying, and he said: "My house, O Muslims." It has already been stated that it is necessary for the subject (<term>mubtada'</term> <gloss>beginning/subject</gloss>) to be [as it is]. Regarding the phrase "What Umar ibn Ma'di Karib has done, how excellent he is in encountering the people of war," and the derivation of that clause: is it permissible or not? I have dispensed with it. Al-Jarmi and a group held the view of permissibility, while al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad held the view of prohibition. This is the chapter on <term>ni'ma</term> <gloss>to praise</gloss> and <term>bi'sa</term> <gloss>to blame</gloss>, and what follows their path in praise and condemnation, such as <term>hubbadha</term> <gloss>how good is</gloss>, <term>sa'a</term> <gloss>how bad is</gloss>, and their peers. They are non-inflected verbs (<term>fi'lan ghayr mutasarrifayn</term> <gloss>static verbs</gloss>). <term>Ni'ma</term> and <term>bi'sa</term> are verbs because the quiescent <term>ta</term> enters them in some dialects, and because of the replacement... al-Kisa'i erred regarding them, and the Kufans held that they are nouns, as reported by the scholars from them in the issues of disagreement. Ibn 'Usfur said: No one has disagreed that they are verbs, and the disagreement is only after they are attributed to the agent. The Basrans say that "The man is good" (<term>ni'ma al-rajul</term>) and "The man is bad" (<term>bi'sa al-rajul</term>) are verbal sentences, whereas al-Kisa'i...</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>...considers them nominal sentences, quoted as phrases, in the position of a proper name like "Ta'abbata Sharran." [He considers them] separated from their origin. They are used for praise and condemnation, elevating two nouns as agents for them, accompanied by the definite article of genus (<term>al-jinsiyya</term> <gloss>the generic article</gloss>), such as "Excellent is the Protector" and "Excellent is the Helper," or added to what he mentioned, meaning added to that which it accompanies, as in his saying "Upon generosity" and "Son of my brother of the people." They elevate a hidden, implied pronoun explained by a <term>tamyiz</term> <gloss>specifying noun/distinction</term> that is singular, such as "Excellent are they as a people" and "Evil is the replacement for the wrongdoers." Sometimes the <term>tamyiz</term> is omitted because the genus of the implied pronoun is known, as in his statement, peace be upon him: "Whoever performs ablution on Friday, it is good and excellent." Al-Akhfash reported that some of the Arabs elevate [the noun] with <term>ni'ma</term> as an indefinite, singular, and added [form], and combined the <term>tamyiz</term> and the manifest agent, such as "Excellent is the man, as a man." There is a famous disagreement among them. Al-Sirafi went to the position of prohibition, because the manifest agent is sufficient and makes the <term>tamyiz</term> unnecessary. Al-Mubarrad went to the position of permissibility.</margin>

## DECLARATION.

Let there be in Figure V two circles, *a, b, c, d* the larger, and *e, f, g, b* the smaller, firmly joined around the same center *i*; *b, d* are their semidiameters; *b, l* and *d, k* are lines equal to the periphery of the larger circle *a, b, c, d*, but *b, m* and *d, n* are lines equal to the periphery of the smaller circle *e, f, g, b*. Having posited these, I say: that the circle is a truly marvelous figure and full of paradoxes.

## DEMONSTRATION.

Since a manifold contradiction of opposites exists in the circle, and indeed: I. By Reason of Generation, while (1) it is made from a mover and the unmoved, for when one end of the semidiameter describing the circle, *d* or *b*, is moved in a circuit, the other *i* rests at the center. While (2) parts of the semidiameter *i, d* moved equally around the center accomplish most diverse spaces in the same time, the furthest from the center the greatest, those closer to the center the least. II. By Reason of the Periphery, which (1) consists of opposites without a medium, of concave and convex without a straight [line]; which (2) although it is finite, yet has the ratio of the infinite within the finite, since the orb of the circular periphery lacks a beginning and an end; for there is no point in which you see its beginning, and none in which you see its end. Which (3) although in actuality it has no discrete angles within itself, is in truth a perpetual and continuous angle, since it is refracted and angled in its individual parts. Which (4) however great it may be, is nevertheless contracted into one central point, and is in a way commensurate with it, since any part of the periphery can be joined with the center through infinite semidiameters. III. By Reason of motion, by which it happens (1) that parts of the circle are moved by contrary motions at the same moment of time; thus when the parts of the circle *g, b* are moved upward toward *a, e*, the parts *b, f* are moved downward toward *d, h*; when the parts *a, e* are moved leftward toward *b, f*, the opposite parts *d, b* move rightward toward *g, e*. Whereby it happens (2) that when all its parts change place, the whole circle nevertheless remains in the same place. Thus, for example, the circle *a, b, c, d* revolved around its center by a motion of gyration does not move locally, for it does not pass from the space it then occupies into another, yet all its parts exercise local motion in that moment.

For if peace is the daughter of war and arms, it cannot be obtained in a bond of marriage, unless by the blood of the combatants. If Peace is the Sun, the light of the world, it is not accustomed to rise unless the Dawn of blood has preceded it. If Peace is the precious pearl of the earth, it does not reach maturity unless it is nourished by a bloody dew. But my speech labors in vain: for the weapons already foreseen from heaven, rushing upon the enemies, will indeed strike, but willingly; they will wound, but those prepared for slaughter; they will maim, but those desiring to die for the love of peace. And because Saint <term>Diva</term> <gloss>Divine/Holy</gloss> URSULA designated that peace should be fashioned in the first naval battle, ships are once again assumed as instruments of peace: for the fates of the Superiors <note>the Heavenly powers</note> decreed that peace be obtained in such a way that nothing but the cruelty of either Maximinus or the Huns should serve the treaties of this peace. One goes, therefore, with a favorable wind, with the Rhine carrying its dear burden, to the destined end of concluding peace. But on the journey, a new delay is cast in the way of peace. For your Holofernes is present, by which, in you, Saint <term>Diva</term> <gloss>Divine/Holy</gloss> URSULA has already betrothed with most certain hope that which you long ago dedicated to heaven with an eternal vow: he meets you, he who designated you as a part of his love, a consort of his Kingdom, and the complement of his happiness. You have him as an adversary, who, though innocently, yet proffers you poison beneath the very honey, hatred beneath love, and ruin beneath fortune: this indeed would have been the mind of Holofernes, had not the vows of URSULA drawn him into her own vows. He would have come to wage war on the Virgin alone, had not the Virgin beseeched virginal peace with prayers. Holofernes would have remained fierce in spirit, had not the Virgin made the Heavenly one <note>referring to a convert, perhaps a symbolic representation of the Hunnish leader's soul</note> royal in deed and in name.

指其竅表
其名叟即
他日示夢
之丈夫可
知矣留之
而自肯滅
之壽始與
之相終交
耳出處之
游之道如

既欲雷之當滅三年壽數始可與君相終始君願之乎
曰願叟乃以兩指捏一竅竅軟如泥隨手而閉二三竅
已曰石上竅數即君壽也作別欲去邢苦雷之辭甚堅
問其姓字亦不言遂去積年餘邢以故他出夜有小偷
入室諸無所失惟竊石而去邢歸悼喪欲死訪察購求
全無蹤緒積有數年偶入報國寺見賣石者近視則其
故物將便認取賣者不服因負石至官官問何所質驗
賣石者能言竅數邢問其他賣石者不能言邢乃言竅

tribus tamen & sororibus hic ad nepotes non extenditur.

### XXI.

Parentes igitur liberis suis absque filijs, fratribus & sororibus defunctis æqualiter, cum relictis fratribus sororibusve utrinque defuncto conjunctis in capita, cum horum verò filijs jure repræsentationis in stirpes succedunt.

### XXII.

Parentes diversæ lineæ ex paterna & materna, pari in gradu constituti, dispares in numero non pro virili portione, sed habita stirpis ratione, sine distinctione bonorum à defuncto relictorum, hæreditatem defuncti hodie dividunt..

### XXIII.

Fratres fratrumque filios ab uno latere defuncto conjunctos ab omnibus ascendentibus excludi, noti juris est.

### XXIV.

Pater adoptivus filij sui adoptivi, quem in potestate non habet, heres esse non poterit, licet filjus ejusmodi ipsi succedat..

### XXV.

Aliud dixerim de illo, in cujus potestatem adoptatus transit, cui sicut arrogatori in bona filij puberis arrogati, ut legitimo & naturali patri, conceditur successio..

### XXVI.

Parentes naturales filijs suis, quos legitimarunt subsequenti matrimonio, vel principis rescripto, vel oblatione curiæ, peræquè succedunt ut naturales & legitimi..

### XXVII.

Qua ratione naturales & spurij suis parentibus, ita hi ipsis vicissim succedunt, nimirum, pater naturalis ejusque ascendentes filio suo naturali in duabus uncijs, mater verò ascendentesque ex linea materna in solidum..

### XXIIX.

Non habet, credo, illud dubium, natos ex incæstu & damnato coitu, si in vivis esse desinant, neque patrem, neque matrem, neque aliquem ascendentium successorem habere..

### XXIX.

Hæc de successione consistentium in linea recta: quibus deficientibus, succedunt in linea obliqua collaterales, quorum successio ad decimum usque gradum porrigitur..

### XXX.

Sed an in feudi antiqui successione agnatorum successio certis gradibus circumscripta sit, an in infinitum procedat, variant Doctorum opiniones propter textus discrepantes, quos distinctionis foedere conciliandos existimo..

### XXXI.

Fratres sororesque <term>ἀμφιθαλεῖς</term> utrinque conjuncti, exclusis ab altero tantùm

tùm latere junctis, ad fratris prædefuncti hæreditatem in capita, concurrentes cum his fratrum utrinque conjunctorum præmortuorum liberi, non alteriores, iure repræsentationis in stirpes vocantur.

### XXXII.

Num quoque in jure feudorum frater consanguineus ab utrinque conjunctis excluditur? Recepta est opinio, unà cum fratre utrinque conjuncto ad defuncti feudum eum esse admittendum.

### XXXIII.

Fratres in feudo paterno sibi invicem succedunt, in novo non ita, sed feudum ad dominum revertitur: utriusque verò sorores sunt incapaces.

### XXXIV.

Si fratrum utrinque conjunctorum filij tantùm extent, neque patrui superstites sint, num ad successionem defuncti patrui in capita, an in stirpes vocantur? Et in capita vocari, tam novo quàm vereri jure obtinuit, & verum est.

### XXXV.

Si defunctus nullos ex utroque latere conjunctos fratres sororésve vel horum filios reliquerit, sed uterinos solummodò vel paternos, tum hi ad fratris hæreditatem admittuntur,

### XXXVI.

Non quidem ut paterna paternis, materna maternis, ut veteri jure, deferantur: sed inter paternos & uterinos, si simul sint, hæreditas defuncti æqualiter diuidatur; si alter tantùm, totam hæreditatem consequatur.

### XXXVII.

Adoptati ab ascendentibus tam ex paterna quàm materna linea ex transuerso sibi invicem succedunt, ut & arrogati, licet hi cognatorum nomine minimè contineantur.

### XXXIIX.

Naturali vinculo se invicem ex patre contingentes collaterales nullo successionis jure fruuntur: per lineam verò maternam conjunctos, etiam-si alter naturalis, alter legitimus sit, sibi invicem succedere, certi juris est.

### XXXIX.

Spurij uno eodemque patre, diversis verò matribus progeniti, sibi invicem succedere prohibentur: quod de ὁμογαστρίοις spurijs nemo affirmabit.

### XL.

Inter incæstuosos fratres, item adoptatos ab extraneo, nulla est successio.

### XLI.

Post fratres fratrumque filios vocantur qui sunt gradu proximiores in capita, ut pares in gradu pariter sine differentia sexus admittantur.

### XLII.

Tantum de successione defunctum cognatione attingentium: quibus

<vocab>feudum, hæreditas, stirpes, consanguineus, uterinos, adoptati, spurij, ὁμογαστρίοις</vocab>

seed:
to the Curia, just as one adopted by a stranger becomes a legitimate successor only to the adopter, not to the other relatives of the father.

### XI.

Other adopted children and the <term>arrogati</term> <gloss>those adopted under the power of another</gloss> who were under the power of the deceased at the time of death, although they succeed together with legitimate and natural children, are by no means admitted to fiefs.

### XII.

What, however, if an adopted son is emancipated by his adoptive father after the death of his natural father; will he lose the succession of both, or will the legitimate inheritance be left to him by the adoptive father? I believe it is fairer to say that all rights of the natural father remain intact for him.

### XIII.

What about those who are natural children only? Justinian willed that these, if no legitimate children or a legitimate wife exist, should succeed to the natural father in two ounces <note>a Roman fractional division of an estate, here one-sixth</note>, to be shared with the mother; but if these are surviving, they are only to be maintained.

### XIIII.

However, we do not grant this right of succeeding in two ounces to grandchildren in the goods of a paternal grandfather or great-grandfather, even if they are legitimate, and the grandfather can rightly institute them as heirs.

### XV.

Such natural children succeed equally to their mother and to those coming from the maternal line, even alongside legitimate children; in fiefs, however, by no means to an illustrious mother.

### XVI.

This succession of natural children has been received everywhere today by a certain interpretation of jurists and by custom, although every concubinage and fornication is illicit and prohibited, and therefore, strictly speaking, there are no natural children today.

### XVII.

Illegitimate children <term>spurij</term> <gloss>children born out of wedlock</gloss> do not succeed to the father <term>ab intestato</term> <gloss>by way of intestacy</gloss> in any manner, neither in allodial lands nor in fiefs, much less to ascendants or those joined through the paternal line; however, it is just that they be provided with sustenance.

### XVIII.

We do not, however, bar them from the succession of their mother and those progressing from maternal origin, unless from an illustrious mother who has legitimate and natural children.

### XIX.

It has been frequently answered that those born from a condemned coitus, for which a penalty is established by law, such as those born from a nefarious, incestuous, or adulterous union, are not successors to the father, nor the mother, nor to those progressing from their line.

### XX.

In the order of ascendants, the right of representation does not have a place; rather, the person who reaches the deceased in a closer degree excludes a more distant one; but in brothers

### XII.

Quid verò, si filius adoptivus post mortem patris naturalis emancipetur à patre adoptivo, utriusque ne successionem perdet, an verò legitima à patre adoptivo ipsi relinquenda erit? æquius opinor erit, si omnia ipsi jura patris naturalis integra reservari dicamus.

### XIII.

Quid de naturalibus liberis tantùm? hos non extantibus legitimis vel uxore legitima, patri naturali in duabus unciis cum matre partiendis succedere Iustinianus voluit: his verò superstitibus, tantùm alendos esse.

### XIIII.

Hoc tamen in duabus unciis succedendi jus nepotibus in avi proavive paterni bonis non concedimus, licet hi legitimi sint, eosque avus rectè instituere possit.

### XV.

Matri verò eiusmodi naturales & à materna linea venientibus æqualiter succedunt, etiam unà cum legitimis: in feudis tamen matri illustri nequaquam.

### XVI.

Hæc naturalium successio interpretatione quadam Iurisprudentum & consuetudine & hodie ubique ferè recepta est, licet omnis concubinatus & scortatio sit illicita & prohibita, ac proinde nulli hodie naturales.

### XVII.

Spurij patri nullo modo ab intestato tam in allodialibus quàm in feudis succedunt, multò minus ascendentibus vel conjunctis per lineam paternam: alimenta tamen ipsis præstanda esse, æquum est.

### XVIII.

Eosdem tamen à matris & ex materna origine progredientium successione non arcemus, nisi à matris illustris, quæ filios legitimos & naturales habeat.

### XIX.

Natos ex coitu damnato, cui à jure pœna constituta est, quales sunt ex nefario, incestuoso & adulterino complexu nati, neque patri, neque matri, & ex linea eorum progredientibus successores esse, sæpius responsum est.

verrammelten Thüren und bewachten die Ihrigen, die ich zuweilen von der Höhe des Pferdes in ängstlicher Spannung in den Höfen zusammen gekauert erblicken konnte. Aus der Ferne hörte man zuweilen Angstrufe von Frauen und Kindern, wenn gewissenlose Marodeurs den Zugang zu den Verstecken derselben erzwungen hatten und sie ausplünderten oder gefangen nahmen.

Die Pâlem unterscheiden sich in ihrer äusseren Erscheinung nicht wesentlich von den Somraï und Gâberi, sind kräftige, ebenmässig gebaute, oft hoch gewachsene Gestalten, von einer mehr oder weniger schwarzen Hautfarbe, die im Allgemeinen keine in's Röthliche oder Gelbliche spielenden Nüancen zeigt, und scheinen ebenfalls grösstentheils die Bagirmi-Sprache zu verstehen.

Der Himmel hatte sich dicht mit Wolken bezogen, und der Donner rollte auf allen Seiten, als wir zu den Füssen einiger Delêb-Palmen ohne sonstigen Baumschutz unser Nachtlager aufschlugen. Die Hälfte der Nacht verbrachtte ich mit der chirurgischen Behandlung der Verwundeten. Die Fleischwunden nähte ich mit Pferdehaaren zusammen und verband die ernsteren Verletzungen so gut es eben ging. Doch Manche hatten penetrirende Brust- und Bauchwunden oder eröffnete Schulter- und Hüftgelenke, und Einige gaben noch in der Nacht den Geist auf.

Am nächsten Morgen (1. Juni) brachen wir eine Stunde vor Sonnenaufgang auf und überschritten, ebenfalls in ungefährer Ostrichtung, eine Niederung mit üppigem Graswuchs, die mir als Komodûgu bezeichnet wurde, an den tiefsten Stellen Sumpfboden und hier und dort kleine Wasserlachen zeigte und sich nach der Aussage der Leute nördlich nach Mul und nordwestlich zum Ba Ili ziehen soll. Ein ähnliches, grasreiches, baumloses und im Sommer wasserreiches Thal, das sich von Südost nach Nordwest zu erstrecken schien, hatten wir Tags zuvor gegen Abend passirt. Beide, sowie die thalähnliche Niederung in der Nähe von Murki und eine andere südsüdwestlich von Gundi gelegene, die wir später zu Gesicht bekamen, scheinen Theile des Sumpfnetzes zu sein, aus dem sich schliesslich der Ba Ili entwickelt. Eine Stunde nach Sonnenaufgang wendeten wir uns südlich, passirten zahlreiche zerstreut liegende und verbarrikadirte Gehöfte, die schon zu Gundi gehörten, zogen über das Centrum dieser Hauptortschaft des Stammes der Tummok hinaus und lagerten um 8 Uhr Morgens. Die unverschämten Sclaven des Königs und seiner höchsten Würdenträger kamen auch reichbeladen zurück, doch meine Leute hatten nur ein Stück Strohzaun erbeutet, das höchstens zur Wandung einer Hütte hinreichte, und wir mussten uns vorläufig mit einer Behausung aus belaubten Zweigen begnügen. Während der Vormittag bei schwachem Südostwind trübe gewesen war, klärte sich um die Mittagszeit der Himmel auf, so dass ich mich der Hoffnung auf eine regenfreie Nacht hingab. Aber die Regenfälle waren mit der Zeit so häufig geworden, und ich konnte so wenig eine Schädigung meiner geringen Habe ertragen, dass ich, als es auch Nachmittags weder Almâs noch Hammu gelungen war, in der Umgegend ein Hüttendach aufzutreiben, mich nicht ohne Sorge zum Schlafen niederlegte.

Es folgte eine böse Nacht, deren Beginn besonders mir in widerwärtiger Erinnerung geblieben ist. Wir hatten, ohne es zu ahnen, meine provisorische Hütte auf einem Termitenbau, der sich noch nicht über das Niveau der Umgebung erhob, errichtet, und Nachts machten mir die verhassten Thierchen einen höchst unliebsamen Besuch. Kaum hatte ich eine halbe Stunde auf meinem stets zu ebener Erde aufgeschlagenen Lager in unruhigem Schlafe verbracht — ich litt seit Somraï an heftigen rheumatischen Schmerzen —, als ich erwachte und ein sonderbares Gefühl auf der Haut meines ganzen Körpers empfand. Ich suchte dasselbe anfangs nicht zu beachten und wieder einzuschlafen, entschloss mich aber doch, da mir meine Schmerzen ohnehin keine Ruhe verhiessen, mich zu erheben und Licht anzuzünden. Letzteres war keine leichte Procedur, denn wenn ich auch aus einem Schälchen mit Butter mittelst eines zu einem Dochte zusammengerollten Fetzchens Châm eine Lampe hergestellt hatte, so war doch unser Kochfeuer erloschen, und ich musste trockene Lumpen an dem Pfannenpulver einer unserer Steinschlossflinten entzünden. Endlich hatte ich Licht und erblickte nun beim trüben Schein der primitiven Lampe mein Lager von Tausenden und Abertausenden weisser Termiten überschwemmt, von denen ich einen grossen Theil bereits erdrückt hatte. Hemd und Oberfläche der Lagerdecke waren mit den zu Brei zerquetschten Insekten bedeckt, und immer neue Schaaren derselben

scenes of the insane attempts to break through the compact mass of the enemy followed: the last short act of the tragedy. But since one could now search the thicket without danger for any women and children still hidden, the general interest was diverted from the last fighters, and while the strife over the possession of the unfortunates, who had lost parents, home, freedom, and hope, flared up on all sides, more disgusting even than the raw horrors of the fight, twenty-some men, the last defenders of Kolî, were able to emerge and, without exactly being maltreated, surrender at discretion. The King of Bagirmi possessed a few hundred more slaves, but a happy, prosperous locality had disappeared from the face of the earth.

Sadly, I rode through the grove past the corpses of the fallen, among whom I also discovered several people who had come with us from Bornû, and across the site of the burned village, where the evidence of an inhuman heroism, as only the highest despair could have evoked in the women of Kolî, constricted the heart of the beholder. Twenty-seven half-burned corpses of infants I counted there, who had been consigned to a violent death by their own mothers in order to preserve them from the almost certain slow demise that would have awaited them in the enemy's war camp, or from long slavery.

After a few hours, we left this scene of bestial devastation. My two boys, Mohammedu and Billama, were nearby with the pack animals and the luggage, and soon most of our fellow travelers from Bornû had also gathered, who almost without exception had obtained a share of the human booty. We marched in an easterly direction through a light forest in which the <term>Delêb</term> palms predominated, until beyond a <term>Pâlem</term> village, which we reached after sunset and whose houses lay scattered far and wide. The inhabitants, although Abû Sekkîn had assured them of his <term>Amân</term> <gloss>formal guarantee of safety/protection</gloss>, had either brought their families to safety in the few cotton trees of the region or had locked them in their poorly barricaded homesteads. Scenen der wahnsinnigen Versuche, die compacte Masse des Feindes zu durchbrechen: der letzte kurze Act des Trauerspiels. Da man aber jetzt ohne Gefahr das Dickicht nach etwa noch versteckten Frauen und Kindern durchsuchen konnte, so wurde das allgemeine Interesse von den letzten Kämpfern abgelenkt, und während der Hader um den Besitz der Unglücklichen, die Eltern, Heimath, Freiheit und Hoffnung verloren hatten, auf allen Seiten entbrannte, ekelhafter als selbst die rohen Gräuel des Kampfes, konnten zwanzig und einige Männer, die letzten Vertheidiger von Kolî, hervorkommen und sich, ohne gerade gemisshandelt zu werden, auf Gnade und Ungnade ergeben. Der König von Bagirmi besass einige hundert Sclaven mehr, aber eine glückliche, wohlhabende Ortschaft war vom Erdboden verschwunden.

Traurig ritt ich durch den Hain an den Leichen der Gefallenen vorbei, unter denen ich auch mehrere mit uns von Bornû gekommene Leute entdeckte, und über die Stätte des verbrannten Dorfes, auf der die Beweise eines unmenschlichen Heroismus, wie ihn nur die höchste Verzweiflung in den Frauen von Kolî hervorgerufen haben konnte, das Herz des Beschauers zusammenschnürten. Siebenundzwanzig halb verbrannte Leichname von Säuglingen zählte ich dort, die von ihren eigenen Müttern einem gewaltsamen Tode überantwortet worden waren, um sie vor dem fast sicheren langsamen Untergange, der ihrer im Kriegslager der Feinde gewartet haben würde, oder langer Sclaverei zu bewahren.

Nach einigen Stunden verliessen wir diesen Schauplatz bestialischer Verwüstung. Meine beiden Knaben Mohammedu und Billama waren mit den Lastthieren und dem Gepäck in der Nähe, und bald hatten sich auch die Meisten unserer Reisegefährten aus Bornû eingefunden, welche fast ohne Ausnahme einen Antheil an der Menschenbeute errungen hatten. Wir marschirten in östlicher Richtung durch einen lichten Wald, in dem die Delêb-Palmen verwalteten, bis über ein Pâlem-Dorf hinaus, das wir nach Sonnenuntergang erreichten, und dessen Häuser weithin zerstreut lagen. Die Bewohner hatten, obgleich Abû Sekkìn sie seines Amân hatte versichern lassen, ihre Familien entweder auf den wenigen Baumwollenbäumen der Gegend in Sicherheit gebracht oder dieselben in ihre nothdürftig verbarrikadirten Gehöfte eingeschlossen. entkrochen der Erde. Alle Stoffe in ihrem Bereich waren bereits durchlöchert und ein quadratisches Stück Châm, das mir als Taschentuch diente, war bis auf unbedeutende Reste verschwunden. Ich stürzte von Ekel übermannt hinaus, weckte Hammu aus dem Schlafe und etablierte mich mit seiner Hülfe innerhalb des Vormittags erbeuteten Stückes Hüttenwandung, über das ich eine Matte und ein Löwenfell deckte. Kaum hatte ich mich von meinem Schrecken erholt, so erhob sich ein Sturmwind aus Ostsüdost, trieb unheildrohende Wolkenmassen herauf, schwächte sich dann ab, und unter rollendem Donner und zuckenden Blitzen ergoss sich ein sündfluthartiger Regen über uns, der mich in einen kläglichen Zustand versetzte und mein Gepäck arg zurichtete.

Erst nach einer Reihe von Tagen gelang es mir, mit Hülfe des Königs in den Besitz einer ausgezeichneten Hütte zu gelangen, welche mich vor den Unbilden der Witterung sicher stellte. Dieselbe liess nicht nur keinen Tropfen selbst des stärksten Regens durch, sondern war mit seltener Kunst hergerichtet. Der Gipfel des Daches bestand in einer grossen, schwach gewölbten Rosette, welche aus rundlichen, dicht geflochtenen, eng mit einander verbundenen Strohkränzen zusammengesetzt und durch Lederstreifen an den eigentlichen Körper des Daches befestigt war. Dieses erschien im Innern glatt, während die freien Enden der zum Flechten verwendeten Strohhalme aussen dicht hervorragten und hier zu einer gleichmässigen Oberfläche sorgfältig verschnitten waren. Diese Acquisition war wichtig, denn Feuchtigkeit und Regenfälle nahmen beständig zu. Während der folgenden Monate Juni und Juli regnete es an mehr als der Hälfte der Tage. Decken und Kleidungsstücke blieben beständig feucht, alles Leder schimmelte, alles Eisen rostete, und selbst Instrumente, welche regelmässig gebraucht wurden, konnten nur mit Mühe frei von Rost gehalten werden. In der Hütte herrschte eine feuchte Kellerluft, und das nöthige Brennmaterial fehlte, um, wie es die Eingeborenen in dieser Jahreszeit zu thun pflegen, ein austrocknendes Feuer zu unterhalten, denn trockenes Holz war selten, und dasselbe in weiter Ferne zu suchen, war bei der Feindseligkeit der Umwohner mit Lebensgefahr verknüpft.

Tummok hatte man mir als das gelobte Land geschildert; Durra, Duchn, Mais, Sesam und Erdnüsse sollten daselbst im Ueberfluss vorhanden und Ziegen und Hühner von unbeschreiblicher Wohlfeilheit sein.

What is to be said about sins against conscience, which truly testifies most sharply that at the time when the sin was committed, we could have done the opposite, or even clearly could have omitted it? *See Regius, chapter 1.* And therefore, unless the will is to suffer the loss of its own liberty, we reject this assertion of Maresius and others entirely.

->§. 21.<-

*Hobbes, in On the Citizen, chapter 14, §. 9*, vehemently confuses moral law with civil law, asserting that the precepts of the Decalogue, especially those of the latter table, are civil laws. Yet those precepts, inscribed upon our hearts, do not depend on any will whatsoever, as civil laws do. Indeed, Hobbes adds that natural laws command the same, but implicitly. Truly, these precepts are also immediately of the Natural Law, and since they are founded according to *Hobbes* on the civil pact by which citizens agree to obedience, they will not even be of natural right by reason of their root, which is absurd.

->§. 22.<-

We do not agree with those who say that simultaneous polygamy is against the law of nature, although many even among our own think so; for it is not an article of faith, so that we can with a safe conscience go over to another opinion; *see Blessed Gerhard, vol. 7, LL., page 106.* For it has not yet been proven by solid reasons to which one could not sufficiently answer. *Thomas, 4 Sentences, dist. 33, q. 1*, distinguishes between the primary law of nature, which arose from the known principles of nature itself, and the secondary, having its origin from conclusions deduced therefrom. ### §. 26.

Injuriosus nimium est *Valla* libro 6. elegantiarum capite 35. in Justinianum Imperatorem, quem nec jura, nec latinas literas novisse, quin quovis ἀναλφαβήτῳ rudiorem fuisse dicit. Quod tamen, quam à vero alienum, ipse imperator §. penultimo prooemii institutionum de se testatur, dum institutiones per compilatores sibi oblatas, ipsemet relegit, et plenissimum robur ipsis addidit, et *Platina* in *Vitis Pontificum* in Bonifacio II. non solum narrat ipsum jura condidisse, sed de Salvatoris quoque nostri incarnatione libros edidisse consignavit. pagina mea 140. Fallitur ergo Valla.

### §. 27.

Carolus Magnus imperium occidentale non accepit per decretum aut potestatem Pontificis Leonis III. sed jure belli, successione à Majoribus, denique tam consensu populi Romani, quam ipsius Imperatoris orientalis. Negant id multi ex Papæis, inter quos *Baronius* in *annalibus ad annum* 800. *Bellarminus in peculiari tractatu.* Nos id cum *Voetio* Parte 2. selectis disputationibus pagina 883. indubitato affirmamus.

### §. 28.

Ea apud plerosque consuetudo obtinuit, ut orationem composituri ab exordio initium faciant, deviantes à more ipsius dicendi Magistri, qui de seipso libro 2. de Oratore scribit: *Omnibus rebus consideratis, tum denique id, quod primum est dicendum, postremo soleo cogitare.* Nam sic demum momenti aliquid afferet, cum erit ex intimis visceribus causæ depromptum, et apparebit, illud penitus ex ea causa, de qua tum agitur effloruisse. Ita sentit etiam Celeberrimus *Vossius* institutionum Oratoriarum libro 3. capite 2. §. 12.

### §. XII.

The head is large because the brain is immune from the obstruction of the nervous tubules; for the jugular vessels transmit a greater abundance of blood to the head, and with the way to the spinal cord closed, the entire nutritive juice flows into the organs of the head; hence the intellect is sharper than is usual for the age, the functions of the brain are unimpaired, and the face is fleshier than in others. Circulation conveniently uses this path to the head; who does not understand that the bones of the cranium are cartilaginous, glutinous, and disjointed above all others in the whole body, especially around the sutures? See Bartholin, <term>Anatomy</term>, p. 699. For the sutures collect these bones. Since the junction of these bones ordinarily happens when infants begin to speak—for speech is indeed impossible without teeth—the present age, while it only promotes teething, easily distends the bones, especially if there is an abundance of nutritive humor in both the falcate and lateral ducts. (In some subjects of 11 months, these ducts admitted a finger, or almost the index finger.)

We mark this disaster in the 3453rd year of the World.

The fifth age comprises an interval of about 588 years, during which the Babylonian captivity was followed by the birth of JESUS CHRIST, so longed for over many centuries; the common Christian Era is usually attributed to Him. When Cyrus, in the first year of the monarchy transferred to the Persians—the 24th of his Persian reign—killed the Babylonian Belshazzar and released the Jewish captivity, he brought an end to the Babylonian servitude which Nebuchadnezzar had imposed upon the Hebrews 70 years prior in the first year of his reign, as the sacred scriptures insinuate (Jeremiah ch. 25 & 29; 2 Chronicles 36:22; 1 Ezra 1:1). ## VI.

### When, therefore, was secular power and jurisdiction granted to bishops and abbots by the Emperors?

<margin>B2.</margin>
Crantz, in Saxony, Book 11, Chapter 23, page 124, writes that Charlemagne gifted regalia to them. Lord Petrus Philippus agrees with him in On Canons, Chapter 6, in the Mirror, page 89. But the opinion of those seems stronger who think that, under the reign of Otto I, they first attained that power in Germany for the most part, because before that time they did not commonly use that power. And Witekind of Corvey mentions, as something new and insolent of that time, that Otto I conferred secular power upon his brother Bruno along with the Archbishopric of Cologne, and likewise made his son Wilhelm Archbishop of Mainz and Prince of Hesse and Thuringia: which is confirmed by many examples and testimonies by Christopher Lehmann, Chronicle of Speyer, page 273. Even if in some places before that time certain bishops had already become secular princes at the same time; for according to Socrates, Book 7, Chapter 7, the Bishop of Alexandria, in the time of Theodosius the Younger, acquired the principate of secular affairs in addition to the lordship of the clergy. The same Socrates, Book 7, Chapter 11, writes also about the Bishop of Rome, that he stepped beyond the limits of the priesthood and had fallen into a secular Principate. ->एकविंशतिपटलः । ४८<-

सुचारुदशनां नित्यां पीनोन्नतपयोधराम् ।
विभङ्गस्थानसंस्थानां महिषासुरमर्दिनीम् ॥ २५ ॥
मृणालायतसंस्पर्शां दशबाहुसमन्विताम् ।
विशूलं दक्षिणेध्येयं खड्गं चक्रं च क्रमात् ॥ २६ ॥
तीक्ष्णां वामतथाशक्तिं बाहुदण्डे विभ्रतीम् ।
खेटकं पूर्णचापञ्च पाशमङ्कुशमुद्रिताम् ॥ २७ ॥
घण्टां वापरमं वापि वामतः सन्निवेशयेत् ।
रक्तचन्दनसिक्ताङ्गीं रक्ताम्बरपरिच्छदाम् ॥ २८ ॥
सिंहस्थां परमेशानीं ब्रह्मविष्णुशिवार्चिताम् ।
प्रेतस्थाञ्च महामायां रक्तपद्मासन स्थिताम् ॥ २९ ॥
सिंहस्थाञ्च तथा दुर्गां ध्यायेत् परममोक्षदाम् ।
शिवः प्रेतोमहादेवो ब्रह्मासोहितपङ्कजः ॥ ३० ॥
विष्णुः सिंह इति ख्यातः वाहनानिमहौजसः ।
स्वमूर्त्त्यावाहनं नैव तेषां देवि प्रयुज्यते ॥ ३१ ॥
तत्तन्मूर्त्त्यन्तरं कृत्वावाहनत्वं गतास्त्वयः ।
शिवप्रेते कदाचित्स्यात्कदाचिद्रक्तपङ्कजे ॥ ३२ ॥
कदाचित्केशरपृष्ठे वसते परमेश्वरि ।
कामकाले शिवप्रेते वसतेसिंहवाहिनी ॥ ३३ ॥
अस्यामहिषमहिष्याः प्रियं सखीगणं शृणु ॥ ३४ ॥

इति श्रीकामिविलास-तन्त्रेएकविंशतिपटलः समाप्तः ।

श्रीतत्पुरुप उवाच ।

चण्डां चण्डवतीं विद्यां चामुण्डां चण्डनायिकां ।
उग्रचण्डां प्रचण्डाञ्च चण्डोयां चण्डनासिकां ॥ १ ॥
शक्तिभिर्वेष्टिता माभिविजयां सिंहवाहिनीं ।
शृणुमन्त्रं प्रवक्ष्यामिमर्हिन्या मोक्षदायकम् ॥ २ ॥
मायाबीजं समुद्धृत्य दुर्गेदुर्गे पदं ततः ।
ततोरुचपदं भद्रे तदन्ते वह्निवल्लभा ॥ ३ ॥
नातः परतरं मन्त्रं लच्यं तन्त्रे सुलोचने ।
दशाक्षरं महामन्त्रं चोद्धृत्य निगदामिते ॥ ४ ॥
मायाबीजं समुद्धृत्य ततोदुर्गेपदं प्रिये ।
वह्निजाया तदन्ते च सर्वसिद्धिप्रदामता ॥ ५ ॥
मायाबीजं समुद्धृत्य दुर्ग्यै तदनन्तरम् ।
वह्निजायां परे दत्त्वा एकधा प्रजपेद्यदि ॥ ६ ॥
कोटि वंस्थान् समादाय वैकुण्ठं स च गच्छति ।
दुर्गे दुर्गे तथाचोक्ता वह्निजाया ततःपरम् ॥ ७ ॥
एषाविद्या महाविद्या चतुर्वर्ग फलप्रदा ।
मायाबीजं समुद्धृत्य तथान्ते वह्निवल्लभा ॥ ८ ॥
एषातवत्तरीविद्या मर्हिन्यादोषवर्जिता ।
ह्रीं दुर्गे तत्तरं मन्त्रं चतुर्वर्ग प्रदायकम् ॥ ९ ॥
ह्रीं दुर्गे रक्षणि पदं नमइत्यच्चरं ततः ।
मायाबीजं समुद्धृत्य वह्निजाया परं तथा ॥ १० ॥
चतुईशाक्षरीविद्या सर्वदोषविवर्जिता ।
ह्रीं दुर्गे तत्तरं मन्त्रं चतुर्वर्गप्रदायकम् ॥ ११ ॥

The reverse logic, the mantra of the other syllable.
The <term>kama-bija</term> <gloss>seed of desire</gloss> and the trident, the sword, and Maya likewise. (15)

Ista sunt sexdecim latera in dicto capite sexagesimo enunciata: quæ perpendi debent iuxta Abrahami Auenetræ sententiam per motum lunæ. Cuius sententiæ subscribimus: vt suprà pernoscere valebis. aduertendum est tutiorem esse crisim quæ in primo tetragono accidit, dein in diametro, & secundo tetragono. In hanc sententiam descendere voluisse videtur Galenus, propterea dicto libro tertio nobis citat quòd lunæ tetragonæ & diametræ stationes in bonis principiis bonas faciunt alterationes, in malis malas, in lethalibus quidem morbis lethales sunt (potissimùm infœliciter affecte) in salubribus bonas inuenire (cum sunt fœliciter affecte) necessum est. Et licet alij imbecilliores sint, attamén magnam decernendi potestatem habent, & in bonum & in malum, pro eorum fortuna aut infortunio: idem de dictis tetragonis & diametris stationibus sentio, propterea illos esse angulares, & non vacuos, cadentes aut intercidentes, (vt quidam medici scribunt) iudicio complectitur Ptolemæus in dicto apotelesmate sexagesimo.

<meta>This page continues the technical breakdown of the lunar cycle in relation to the "critical days" of an illness, specifically mapping the Moon’s movement through the zodiac signs of Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, and Scorpio. The previous page likely established the starting point of this calculation.</meta>

# OF THE CRITICAL DAYS

<margin>H</margin>
The Moon’s movement to the fourteenth degree of Taurus will be the eighth side, and the eighth day, which is the Moon’s diametrical position <note>original: "diametralis lunæ statio." This refers to an opposition aspect, occurring at 180 degrees from the starting point.</note>.

<margin>I</margin>
The Moon’s passage to the fourteenth degree of Gemini will be the ninth side, and the ninth day, and the second trigonal <note>a trine aspect, occurring at 120 degrees</note> position.

<margin>K</margin>
The twenty-ninth degree of the Twins <note>Gemini</note> will be the tenth side, and the tenth <term>critical day</term> <note>A day of crisis (from the Greek *krinein*, to judge) where a patient’s illness is expected to take a definitive turn for better or worse.</note>. For it is the half of the square irradiation <note>original: "irradiationis tetragonæ," or a quadrate aspect of 90 degrees</note> with respect to the aforementioned diametrical irradiation and the second square.

<margin>L</margin>
The Moon’s progression to the fourteenth degree of Cancer will be the eleventh side, and the eleventh "judiciary" day <note>original: "dies iudicatiuus," a day providing signs that allow the physician to judge the future course of the disease</note>; for it is the third hexagonal <note>a sextile aspect, occurring at 60 degrees</note> position of the Moon.

<margin>M</margin>
The fourteenth degree of Leo (provided the Moon reaches that exact degree—otherwise it would not judge, and the same rule for judging applies to other aspects) will be the twelfth side, and the twelfth day, and the second quadrangular <note>square</note> position.

<margin>N</margin>
The fourteenth degree of Virgo will be the thirteenth side, and the thirteenth critical day, and the third lunar triangle <note>trine aspect</note>.

<margin>O</margin>
The twenty-ninth degree of Virgo will be the fourteenth side, and the fourteenth critical day, and the half-part of the aspect after the second square.

<margin>P</margin>
The fourteenth degree of Libra will judge; it is the Moon’s fourth hexagonal radiation, the fifteenth side, and the fifteenth day.

<margin>Q</margin>
From there <note>original: "inde," the catchword from the previous page</note>, the Moon’s progress again to the fourteenth degree of Scorpio will make the sixteenth critical day.

<summary>This page lists the specific zodiacal degrees and lunar aspects (squares, trines, and sextiles) that determine the critical days of a disease's progression. It tracks the Moon from Taurus through Scorpio, defining which days will offer a "judgment" on the patient's health.</summary>

<margin>3)</margin>
§. 12. His accedit (3) connexio finis ultimi actionum nostrarum cum mediis ad eum ducentibus. Certus quippe est finis ultimus, certa beatitudo, certum <term>brabeion</term> nostrum. Natura verò universis hominibus ingeneravit desiderium summi boni et beatitudinis consequendæ. Quod si igitur via ad beatitudinem illam foret incerta et contingens, non frustra tantùm, verùm etiam fraudulenter et insipienter illud desiderium homini ingeneratum esset.

<margin>4)</margin>
Denique (4) mirum esset immò divinæ sapientiæ et bonitati inconveniens, dari in rebus naturalibus et quibus homo carere quadantenus potest, tantam rationum firmitatem, ut in iis locus detur demonstrationibus; in rebus fidei autem et quæ salutem concernunt, non dari. Ex quibus satis liquet, non solùm animi sed et actionum nostrarum firmam esse certitudinem. Hinc rectè *Plutarchus in Timoleonte, p. m. 438. juxta versionem Xylandri: Oportet non solùm ipsam actionem justam honestamque: sed etiam consilium, quo inducti eam suscipimus,* (νόμιμος καὶ ἀμετάπτωτος δόξα) *constans esse et immobile et cetera.* Quò facit, quod *Cicero libro 1. de Officiis* ait: *Benè præcipiunt, qui vetant quidquam agere, quod dubites æquum an iniquum sit.* Quæ cum ita sint, patet ad oculum, quam absurdum sit et impium Probabilistarum dogma, venditans *Probabilitatem* pro regula ac norma actionum moralium et conscientiæ. Neque enim vel ulla ratio probabilis, vel ullius doctoris auctoritas; sed Lex divina, tùm cordibus hominum inscripta, tùm in verbo revelata, eaque in se certissima ac animo firmo fideque indubitata recepta, sola est Conscientiæ actuumque Christianorum regula ac in rebus præfertim cultum Dei et salutem animæ concernentibus, nulla prorsus probabilis ratio sufficit, sed requiritur fides divino testimonio firmiter inhærens. Benè igitur *Ambrosius* ad istud Apostoli: *Omne quod non est ex fide, peccatum est,* ait: *Peccatum est, quod aliter fit, quàm probatum est* (scilicet in verbo Dei.) Item *Augustinus* super eundem locum. *Omne quod aliter fit, quàm probatum est, peccatum est.* Prout hæc Patrum dicta citantur in Corpore Canonico, Canon Omnes. Causa XXVIII. Quaestio I.

faith is born of a good and tranquil conscience (such as the Apostle requires). Hence from the same Pauline passage the Moralists themselves, and especially *Laymann (Book 1, Theol. Mor. Treatise 1, Chapter 5, § 1)* and with him many others whom he cites, commonly assert that for acting rightly or honestly, a practically and morally certain judgment is required, by which all fear of the opposite is excluded. And he proves it: *Whoever deliberately commits himself to the danger of sinning, he sins: but whoever acts while not practically certain whether he is acting rightly and honestly, he commits himself to the danger of practically erring or sinning: Therefore, etc.* And so stands this Assertion of Laymann, which he placed in the very first position: *To do or omit something with a doubt that is properly practical is always a sin.* And he says that this is the common sentiment, which is proven from Romans 14: *Whatever is not from faith is sin.* Furthermore, the same Paul in the same Chapter XIV to the Romans, v. 5, commands: *<term>hékastos en tōi idíōi noï plērophoreísthō</term>*, i.e., let each one be fully certain in his own mind. I know indeed that the Vulgate renders it: *Let each one abound in his own sense.* But wrongly, for that version, as Justinianus himself admits, gave occasion for error. And to abound in one's own sense is a vice and of a brazen front, as *Salmeron* asserts. *<term>plērophoreísthai en idíōi noï</term>* is not to abound in one's own sense, but to have certainty in one's mind, and it denotes the most firm cognition and persuasion of the mind, so that the mind may be clearly *<term>ametáptōtos</term>* <gloss>unwavering</gloss> in that cognition, as this word is used in Luke I, 1. Hence *Luther* rightly translates: **Let everyone be certain in his own opinion.** Where in the margin: **He should not waver or doubt in his conscience, etc.** From which passages it appears that the Apostle requires such *<term>plērophoría</term>* <gloss>full assurance</gloss> and certainty of mind, by which a Christian man may be certain and full of confidence that what is to be done is approved by God.

§ 11. But just as our mind ought to be certain in its actions, so also there must be a certain degree of certainty and necessity in morals and duties. Aristotle indeed, whom the Jesuits value highly in this controversy in particular, in *Book I of the Nicomachean Ethics*, denies that there is *<term>t’akribés</term>* <gloss>the accurate/precision</gloss>, i.e., precision or anything accurate, in moral conclusions; but rather that error is so inherent in just and honest things that they seem established by law, not by nature. It is therefore as if he had said, as his disciples say today: *probability reigns in moral matters.* But let us forgive [them] for the time being.

when the girls, the care of Heaven, exult at his gifts and guard the flower of their fleeting age.
<margin>The festive fireworks were displayed on the Pincian Hill at the roots of the Temple of the Most August Trinity,</margin>
Why should the heavenly ones vibrate thunderbolts, if the scaffolds pleasing to the Thunderer serve the honor of the Divine Trinity, licking the ambitious footprints of the sacred temple? What of the fact that the earth flatters the starry Foster-child, the Dauphin, leaping up: if Martial Rome celebrates the gifts of Heaven, far be the clouds, far be the rain, and the South winds. He had spoken, and to him the King of the air adds against these things. Spare your fear, most faithful guardian of the French Kingdom, these clouds do not portend war to the Romulides <note>Romans</note>, and to your Dauphin: the foreign sea will cling to the clouds, nor will it move its journey to the realms of Neptune. Nay, the damages themselves will help more, and the dangers themselves will help more, bearing witness to the God the guardian, who with a favorable divine will fortifies the French joys of the applauding Rome. It was profitable to cover the stars with a blackening mantle, lest Cynthia comprehend Heaven with her beautiful face, rivaling the missiles of flames, which the Aetna of Quirinus <note>Rome</note> will pour out wide, pregnant with harmless sulfur. You, golden sister of Phoebus, will press the rose-colored chariot with a cloud, when Rome opens the theater, competing with the dwellers of heaven:
<margin>After the fire-game was finished, the clouds scattered and the Moon revealed herself.</margin>
Soon when the most beautiful mother of flames has yielded to the frequent thunderbolts and the returning fire, behold, Lucina <note>the moon/goddess of childbirth</note> will again dissolve the shadows, shining, the white Cynthia, directress of the starry night. §. 3. Furthermore, the Sacred History sufficiently teaches what end GOD, the Best and Greatest, had proposed for Himself in this miracle. Namely, so that He might satisfy the desire of *Joshua*, He granted to those about to destroy the *Amorites* completely a longer enjoyment of solar light than nature would otherwise have permitted. Nor, indeed, would the same thing happen to the *Israelites* that history testifies has occurred quite often elsewhere, namely, that the intervening night should set an end and measure to the victory. Just as we have heard it happened in that most memorable battle of *Aetius* with *Attila*, according to *Paul the Deacon, book 15*. But that could not have happened (all other things being equal) unless the Sun had been hindered in its primary motion. Indeed, many causes can be given, even those encountered in nature, for why one day exists longer than another, not only for the different reason of one day compared to different polar altitudes, but also in the same latitude of a place. For, in the first place, the *Sun's* own proper motion can increase the day somewhat. Hence the day of the *Sun* is greater than the day of the primum mobile <note>original: "primi mobilis" <gloss>the sphere of the fixed stars, the outermost rotating heaven</gloss></note> by a few minutes, just as it is also longer than the sidereal [day], which is the same as this, or at any rate not longer than a pulse beat of a human artery. Then, *Refraction* is no less important, which, although often ignored, is a true cause of wondrous effects just as it is elsewhere, and so it can also make the day longer. For since it raises the stars by its very nature, and procures for them a greater altitude than they truly have, especially at a greater distance from the zenith: it therefore offers the Sun to our eyes much sooner on the eastern horizon, and indeed before it has truly risen. And meanwhile, concerning Christ Jesus, his Gospel, and his benefit, concerning faith, charity, mercy, clemency, and sincerity, there is no word at all. Unless, perhaps, we wish to be content with that extraordinary doctrine*

Regarding this, the *Lushi* <note>Grand History</note> says that Shun herded sheep at Huangyang, burned pottery at Changyang, fashioned utensils at Shouqiu, and lived at Fuxia. The *Mujie* <note>Chronicle of Wood</note> also says he lived at Fuxia. Zheng Xuan says: "Fuxia is a place name." The *Suoyin* <note>Search for Obscurities</note> says: "To live at a time is to pursue the time, as if to say seizing the opportunity to seek profit." The *Shangshu Dazhuan* <note>Great Commentary on the Book of Documents</note> says: "Summer days spent trading at Dunqiu, living at Fuxia." Mencius says: "He moved to Fuxia, traded at Dunqiu, and borrowed at Chuanxu." These events have never been exhausted; they can supplement the legacy of his plowing and farming.

Wen River and Mount Tai

The Wen River is south of Qi and north of Lu, the boundary of the two states. Of the rivers in the two states, the Wen is the largest. South of Mount Tai is Lu, and north of it is Qi. The territory of the two states is divided by the Dai <note>Mount Tai</note>. Of the mountains in the east, the Dai is the ancestor. This commentary on the Wen River was obtained from the Xing commentary <note>邢疏, referring to Xing Bing's commentary</note>, but the previous commentary on Mount Tai did not rely on the Kong commentary <note>孔疏, referring to Kong Yingda's commentary</note> on the *Classic of Poetry*, which is a loss of half the truth.

The taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, and tongue-contact as a condition for the various feelings born of it are perceived as being like an illusion, like a transformation, and like a dream. Celestial sons, you should know that the body-element is perceived as being like an illusion, like a transformation, and like a dream. Celestial sons, you should know that the mind-element is perceived as being like an illusion, like a transformation, and like a dream. The mental-object-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and mind-contact, as well as mind-contact as a condition for the various feelings born of it are perceived as being like an illusion, like a transformation, and like a dream. Why is this? Because the mind-element and the others have an empty self-nature. First, the "mirror of reality as empty." It is separated from all marks of the realms of the mind. There are no phenomena that can be manifested. It is not an object of awakening and illumination. 
The first part clarifies that in <term>Tathata</term> <gloss>Thusness</gloss>, deluded phenomena do not exist originally. They do not exist beforehand and later disappear; therefore, it is called "reality as empty." The following explains the meaning of emptiness. The inverted mind and deluded realms never corresponded originally, hence it is said to be "separated from, etc." It does not mean it exists but does not manifest. It is just that, in principle, deluded phenomena do not exist, so there is nothing that can be manifested.
